name: The Three-Body Problem
blurb: Liu Cixin's science fiction novel of humanity's first contact with an alien civilization
title: The Three-Body Problem Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending
description: The Three-Body Problem summary: Ye Wenjie, Wang Miao and Shi Qiang, the Red Coast base, the VR game, the ETO and sophons, and how Liu Cixin's novel ends.
h1: The Three-Body Problem: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: The Three-Body Problem (三体) is a science fiction novel by the Chinese writer Liu Cixin, serialized in 2006 and published as a book in 2008; Ken Liu's 2014 English translation won the 2015 Hugo Award for Best Novel. It moves between China's Cultural Revolution in the 1960s and the early 21st century. In the present, a nanomaterials scientist is drawn into a police investigation of a wave of suicides among physicists and a strange virtual-reality game. The past story follows an astrophysicist whose work at a secret military base turns out to be connected to it all.

body: The past, 1967 onward: Ye Wenjie watches Red Guards beat her father, the physicist Ye Zhetai, to death at a public struggle session, while her mother denounces him. Sent to a forestry labor corps in Inner Mongolia, Ye reads Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, lent by the journalist Bai Mulin, and begins to doubt that humanity can correct its own evil. When a letter she copied for Bai is discovered, he lets her take the blame. Instead of prison she is taken to Red Coast, a secret military base on a mountain, whose hidden purpose is to search for and contact extraterrestrial life. Ye discovers that the Sun can amplify radio signals and, without authorization, uses it to send a message into space. Eight years later a reply arrives from a single alien listener on a world called Trisolaris, warning her not to answer again or her planet will be conquered. Alone in the control room, Ye answers anyway and invites them to come.

The present: Wang Miao is approached by Shi Qiang and a group of military officers, led by General Chang, who say that leading scientists have been killing themselves, including Yang Dong, who left a note saying physics does not exist. Soon Wang sees a countdown in every photograph he takes and then in his own vision. A woman tied to a scientific society called the Frontiers of Science tells him it will stop if he halts his nanomaterials project. He then watches the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the Big Bang, flicker in time with the countdown.

Wang begins playing Three Body, a virtual-reality game set on a planet whose three suns move unpredictably, producing Stable Eras when civilization can grow and Chaotic Eras of deadly heat or cold that destroy it. Players meet versions of famous figures such as King Wen of Zhou and Mozi, and in one level Newton and von Neumann turn Qin Shi Huang's army of millions into a human computer to predict the suns' motion. Wang works out that the planet orbits a three-star system whose motion has no general solution. Players who reach the higher levels are invited to real meetings, where Wang learns that Trisolaris is real and that the game is a recruiting tool for the Earth-Trisolaris Organization, a secret movement of people disillusioned with humanity. Its commander is Ye Wenjie. Its main factions are the Adventists, led by Mike Evans, who want the aliens to destroy humanity, and the Redemptionists, who see the Trisolarans almost as gods to be saved.

It also emerges that, soon after receiving the alien warning, Ye killed her husband, the engineer Yang Weining, and the commissar Lei Zhicheng, the two people who could have exposed her. Tipped off by Wang, Shi and the army raid an ETO gathering and arrest her. Evans keeps the actual messages from Trisolaris aboard his ship, Judgment Day. Following Shi's plan, the military strings ultra-thin nanofilaments made from Wang's material across the Panama Canal, and as the ship passes through, the filaments slice it and everyone aboard into pieces, leaving the computer data intact.

The recovered messages reveal the rest. A Trisolaran fleet has already set out and will reach Earth in about four hundred and fifty years. To stop humanity from advancing in that time, Trisolaris has sent sophons: protons unfolded into vast circuits, refolded and sent to Earth, where they sabotage particle accelerator experiments, which explains the scientists' despair, and produce the countdown and flickering sky.

Trisolaris sends a final contemptuous message telling humanity that they are bugs. Wang and other scientists are crushed, convinced that fundamental science has been frozen and that humanity cannot win. Shi Qiang, who has no scientific training, drives Wang out to the countryside and shows him fields swarming with locusts. Humans, he points out, have tried to wipe out insects with every weapon they have, and the bugs have never been defeated. Wang decides to return to work.

Read on its own, the ending is cautiously hopeful: technological inferiority is not the same as defeat, and ordinary stubbornness matters. It is also a setup, since the war itself lies centuries ahead and is the subject of the two sequels. Ye Wenjie's choice to invite an alien invasion is the other point readers argue about. Some see her as a tragic figure whose despair was created by the violence she witnessed; others see her as the novel's villain, betraying all of humanity because of what some people did. The book presents her reasons without endorsing them, and how to judge her is debated.

ul: Faith and despair about humanity: Ye's experience of the Cultural Revolution leads her to believe only an outside force can save or punish humankind.
Science under attack: the sophons and the suicides show what happens when the foundation of research is taken away.
Chaos and survival: Trisolaris's unpredictable suns explain why its civilization is ruthless and desperate to leave.
Ordinary courage: Shi Qiang, a policeman with no theory, often sees more clearly than the scientists.
Environmentalism and its extremes: Silent Spring and Mike Evans show concern for nature turning into hatred of humans.
Length: about 400 pages in English translation; it is the first book of the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy, followed by The Dark Forest (2008) and Death's End (2010).
Original language: Chinese. The Chinese book edition places the Cultural Revolution chapters in the middle; the English translation opens with them.

Adaptations: the Chinese series Three-Body (Tencent, 2023), which follows the novel closely, and the English-language series 3 Body Problem (Netflix, 2024), which moves much of the story to Britain and combines characters.
Content advisory: political violence and a killing at the opening, suicide, and a mass killing aboard a ship.

check.q: Who first answers the alien message and invites the Trisolarans to Earth?
check.why: Alone at Red Coast Base, Ye Wenjie replies despite the warning and invites them to come.

check.q: What is the Three Body virtual-reality game really for?
options: A recruiting tool for the Earth-Trisolaris Organization
check.why: Players who reach high levels are invited to real ETO meetings.

check.q: How is the ship Judgment Day captured?
options: Nanofilaments strung across the Panama Canal slice it apart
It is boarded by soldiers in open sea
check.why: Shi Qiang's plan uses filaments made from Wang's nanomaterial so the ship's data survives.

faq.q: What are sophons in The Three-Body Problem?
faq.a: Sophons are protons that the Trisolarans turned into supercomputers and sent to Earth, where they interfere with particle accelerators and spy on humanity to freeze its progress in physics.

faq.q: Why does Ye Wenjie betray humanity?
faq.a: After seeing her father killed and the cruelty of the Cultural Revolution, and after reading about environmental destruction, she concludes humanity cannot reform itself and hopes an alien civilization will.

faq.q: Should I read the book or watch the Netflix series first?
faq.a: The novel and the Tencent series tell the same Chinese story; the Netflix series changes settings, merges characters and draws on the later books.
